n: Nathan’s warning that trouble would rise from David’s own house begins to come true. Amnon, David’s eldest son, becomes obsessed with his half-sister Tamar, the full sister of Absalom.

f.g: “Palm tree.” She and Absalom were children of Maacah (2 Samuel 3:3); Amnon was born to Ahinoam.
As the story shows, this was lust, not true love.

n: Amnon’s desire makes him sick with frustration. As an unmarried princess, Tamar was closely protected, so he saw no way to get to her.

f.g: Vexed = distressed, tormented.

n: Amnon’s cousin Jonadab, a clever and scheming man, enters the story.

f.g: Subtil = shrewd, crafty — the same quality used of the serpent in Genesis 3:1.
Also called Shammah, one of David’s older brothers.

n: Jonadab notices Amnon looking haggard and asks why. Amnon admits his desire for Tamar.

f.g: Thin, run-down, looking ill.

n: Jonadab devises a plan: pretend to be sick and ask the king to send Tamar to prepare food for him. It uses David’s care for his children against him.

f.g: Food in general.

n: Amnon follows the plan exactly and asks David for Tamar to bake him special cakes.

f.g: Possibly heart-shaped cakes or dumplings; the Hebrew word sounds like the word for “heart.”

n: David, unsuspecting, sends Tamar to help her brother. The king who once sent for Bath-sheba now unknowingly sends his daughter into danger.

f.g: Prepare food for him.

n: Tamar obediently goes and prepares the food in Amnon’s presence, as requested.
Amnon refuses to eat and orders everyone else to leave the room, isolating Tamar.

f.w: Have out all men from me
f.g: Send everyone out.

n: He asks Tamar to bring the food into his inner room so he can eat from her hand.
When she comes close, he grabs her and demands she sleep with him.
Tamar resists with dignity and clear moral reasoning: this is forbidden in Israel and would be a disgraceful, senseless act.

f.g: Do not humiliate or violate me.

f.w: no such thing ought to be done in Israel

f.g: Hebrew nebalah — a shameful outrage, a serious moral crime.

n: Tamar pleads: she would carry lifelong shame, and he would be counted among Israel’s worst fools. She even suggests asking the king for marriage — likely trying anything to escape.

f.w: he will not withhold me from thee
f.g: Though the law forbade such a marriage, Tamar may simply be desperate to buy time.

n: Amnon refuses to listen and, being stronger, rapes her. The narrator states it plainly, with no attempt to excuse it. The blame lies entirely with Amnon.
Immediately his “love” turns to intense hatred, revealing it was only selfish lust. He orders her out.

f.w: the hatred wherewith he hated her
f.g: Lust that uses another person often turns to contempt once satisfied.

n: Tamar protests that throwing her out is an even greater wrong, since it leaves her disgraced and abandoned without any protection. He still won’t listen.

f.g: Possibly “No!” or “There is no reason for this.”

n: Amnon calls a servant to throw “this woman” out and lock the door — he no longer even uses her name.

f.g: In Hebrew simply “this one” — a dehumanizing term.

n: Tamar wears the special robe of a royal virgin daughter. The servant puts her out and bolts the door.

f.g: Divers = various. Perhaps a long robe with sleeves, worn by the king’s unmarried daughters — the same rare phrase as Joseph’s coat.

n: Tamar shows her anguish publicly: ashes on her head, her royal robe torn, her hand on her head, crying aloud. She refuses to hide what was done to her.

f.g: A sign of deep mourning and grief.

f.w: laid her hand on her head
f.g: A gesture of grief or shame.

n: Absalom guesses what happened and tells Tamar to keep quiet for now. She lives the rest of her life desolate in his house — a deep injustice that no one in authority remedies.

f.g: Be quiet; don’t speak of it.
Alone, ruined, without marriage or future.

n: David is very angry, but he does nothing. The Greek Septuagint adds that he would not punish Amnon because he loved him as his firstborn. David’s failure to act sets up the next tragedy.

f.g: Wroth = angry. David’s own sin may have weakened his moral authority to discipline his sons.

n: Absalom says nothing at all to Amnon, but he hates him and quietly plans revenge.

f.g: An idiom for nothing at all.

n: Two years later, Absalom holds a sheep-shearing festival — a time of feasting — and invites all the king’s sons.

f.g: Sheep-shearing was a festive occasion with food and drink (1 Samuel 25:2-8).
A place about 15 miles north of Jerusalem.

n: Absalom invites the king himself and his officials, perhaps knowing he would decline.
David declines so as not to be a burden, but gives Absalom his blessing.

f.g: A financial burden.

n: Absalom then asks that Amnon, the crown prince, come in David’s place. David seems uneasy.

f.w: Why should he go with thee?
f.g: David may sense something is wrong.

n: Absalom presses until David agrees to send Amnon and all his sons.

f.g: Urged him insistently.

n: Absalom orders his servants to kill Amnon when he is drunk, assuring them they act under his authority.
Absalom’s servants murder Amnon at the feast. The other princes flee in terror on their mules.

f.g: Mules were ridden by royalty in David’s time.

n: A false report reaches David first: all his sons have been killed.
David tears his clothes and lies on the ground in grief, and his servants do the same.

f.g: Tare = tore.

n: Jonadab — who had helped Amnon plan the crime — now coolly tells David that only Amnon is dead, revenge Absalom had planned since Tamar’s rape. Jonadab seems to know far too much.

f.g: By Absalom’s order or determination.

n: Jonadab reassures the king that he need not grieve as though all his sons were dead.
Absalom flees. A watchman sees a crowd coming down the hillside road.

f.w: the young man that kept the watch
f.g: A lookout posted on the city wall.

n: Jonadab points out the king’s sons arriving, just as he said.
The princes arrive weeping, and David and all his servants weep bitterly with them.
Absalom takes refuge with his grandfather, King Talmai of Geshur. David mourns every day — whether for Amnon or for his estranged son Absalom.
Absalom remains in Geshur for three years.

f.g: A small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee.

n: Over time David comes to terms with Amnon’s death and longs to see Absalom again. The Hebrew is uncertain; it may mean David’s anger toward Absalom faded.

f.w: longed to go forth unto Absalom
f.g: Some translations read “ceased to go out against Absalom” — his hostility eased.
